bib.title: Symbol tuning improves in-context learning in language models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Symbol Tuning Improves In-Context Learning in Language Models", Jerry Wei, Le Hou, Andrew Lampinen, Xiangning Chen, Da Huang, Yi Tay, Xinyun Chen, Yifeng Lu, Denny Zhou, Tengyu Ma, Quoc V. Le (Google, Stanford). arXiv:2305.08298v2, dated 30 Dec 2023 (the PDF header reads January 2, 2024). The printed first-page note gives no venue, so treat it as a preprint (EMNLP 2023 is not stated in the text I read). The paper dates from 2023.

COVERAGE: The PDF has 89 pages and 212,382 characters. I read the main text (pp. 1-11) and Appendix A.1-A.8 (pp. 18-23) in full. I only skimmed Appendices B-E: dataset lists, symbol selection, prompt formats, per-task tables D.1-D.5 and the prompt dumps E.1-E.4 (pp. 24-89). I did not read the per-task numbers or the prompt dumps, so I make no claims from them. I did not skim the references for origins beyond what the text credits.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Method (what to teach): symbol tuning means finetuning on in-context input-label pairs with instructions removed and labels replaced by arbitrary symbols. The model then has to infer the task from the exemplars.
  number: none
  setup: 22 classification datasets, 2-10 exemplars per class, ~30k tuning symbols (integers, character combinations, words). Models are Flan-PaLM 8B, 62B, Flan-cont-PaLM-62B and 540B.
  quote: "we finetune language models on input–label pairs presented in-context where natural language labels are remapped to arbitrary symbols."
  where: p.2
- Gains concentrate where the prompt gives no natural-language labels: +5.5 to +15.5 points without relevant labels, +0.8 to +4.2 with them.
  number: +11.1 (62B-c, no labels and no instruction), +9.3 (540B, no labels, with instruction)
  setup: Average accuracy over 11 unseen tasks, 4 exemplars per class, at most 100 eval examples per task. Four settings cross instruction present/absent with relevant label present/absent. Claim holds for models 62B and larger.
  quote: "small improvements in settings with relevant natural language labels (+0.8% to +4.2%) and substantial improvements in settings without relevant natural language labels (+5.5% to +15.5%)."
  where: p.5, Table 1
- Table 1 rows (relevant labels / instructions columns ✓✓, ✓✗, ✗✓, ✗✗): Flan-PaLM-540B scores 82.2, 77.4, 70.7, 58.1 and symbol-tuned scores 84.4, 78.8, 80.0, 63.6. Random guessing is 42.4.
  number: 58.1 to 63.6 (540B, hardest setting)
  setup: as above
  quote: "Flan-PaLM-540B 82.2 77.4 70.7 58.1 + Symbol tuning (ours) 84.4 ( +2.2) 78.8 ( +1.4) 80.0 ( +9.3) 63.6 ( +5.5)"
  where: p.5
- Symbol tuning lets a smaller model match a larger one on label-from-exemplar learning, which the authors equate to about 10x less inference compute.
  number: ~10x
  setup: no-relevant-label settings, 11 tasks
  quote: "symbol-tuned Flan-PaLM-8B outperforms Flan-PaLM-62B, and symbol-tuned Flan-PaLM-62B outperforms Flan-PaLM-540B."
  where: p.5
- Symbol tuning hurts small models when the labels are meaningful. Flan-PaLM-8B drops with relevant labels, which the authors attribute to overfitting or to treating all labels as arbitrary.
  number: -6.3 (✓✓), -7.3 (✓✗)
  setup: Flan-PaLM-8B, Table 1
  quote: "57.6 ( -6.3) 54.3 ( -7.3)"
  where: p.5
- Algorithmic transfer: gains on tasks never seen in tuning, with no numeric or algorithmic data in the tuning mix.
  number: list functions +18.2 (8B), +11.1 (62B), +15.5 (62B-c), +3.6 (540B). Simple Turing concepts +15.3 (8B and 62B), +14.1 (62B-c), +4.7 (540B).
  setup: BIG-Bench list functions (top 20 by human accuracy, 4-shot) and simple Turing concepts (ASCII subset, ≤3 instructions). Gains shrink with model size.
  quote: "symbol tuning results in an average performance improvement across all tasks of 18.2% for Flan-PaLM-8B, 11.1% for Flan-PaLM-62B, 15.5% for Flan-cont-PaLM-62B, and 3.6% for Flan-PaLM-540B."
  where: p.6
- Flipped labels: instruction tuning destroys the ability to follow in-context labels that contradict priors, and symbol tuning restores it. Even so, the result is not clearly above chance on average.
  number: +26.5 (8B), +33.7 (62B), +34.0 (540B)
  setup: 6 binary tasks (ADEC, OR, SUBJ, TC, TEH, TOS). Labels are flipped in the exemplars and in the eval example, and no flipped labels appear in tuning.
  quote: "Flan-PaLM-8B sees an average improvement across all datasets of 26.5%, Flan-PaLM-62B sees an improvement of 33.7%, and Flan-PaLM-540B sees an improvement of 34.0%."
  where: p.7
  caveat quote: "performance on the flipped-labels settings is, on average, not significantly better than random guessing."
- Cheap to run: the big changes occur in the first 1k-2k steps.
  number: 1k steps ≈ 16 min (8B, 64 TPUv4 chips), 70 min (62B, 128 chips), 6 h (540B, 512 chips)
  setup: 8B and 62B tuned up to 10k steps, 540B up to 5k. 540B performance drops after 1k steps.
  quote: "the largest changes in performance occur within the first 1k to 2k steps of symbol tuning, after which model performance stays relatively constant."
  where: p.8; timings p.4
- A small symbol-tuning share (e.g. 16%) is enough for the in-context learning (ICL) gains, but flipped-label ability keeps rising with the share of symbol data. The authors default to 100% symbol data.
  number: 16%
  setup: mixtures with instruction-tuning data from Chung et al. 2022 (8B, 62B, 62B-c; 540B excluded)
  quote: "even a small mixture of symbol- tuning data (e.g., 16%) versus instruction-tuning data can significantly change model performance."
  where: pp.8-9
- Diversity matters: more tuning datasets are better, and tuning on only 1-2 datasets helps no-label settings but hurts relevant-label settings.
  number: 22 datasets vs 0, 1, 2, 5, 11
  setup: 8B, 62B, 62B-c, 4k steps
  quote: "symbol tuning works best when a large variety of tasks are used, and symbol tuning with only a small number of tasks may result in models that perform worse in settings with relevant labels."
  where: p.10
- Control: the gain is from the symbol data, not from extra tuning steps. Continued instruction tuning for the same steps gives little or negative change.
  number: for example 540B flipped labels 19.2 (instruction-tuned) vs 54.7 (symbol-tuned); 62B turing 54.1 vs 76.5
  setup: Table 2, same step counts
  quote: "we conclude that the symbol-tuning data itself is the root cause of the results we observed in this paper."
  where: p.18
- Symbol tuning is no help with one exemplar per class unless the model has been symbol-tuned: the gap is largest there.
  number: none (read from Figure 14, which gives no printed numbers)
  setup: hardest setting (no labels, no instruction), 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 exemplars per class
  quote: "In this setting, symbol- tuned models perform much better than base models, and this trend is consistent across all of our tested models."
  where: p.21
- Benchmarks are unchanged for large models: MMLU (5-shot) and BIG-Bench Hard (3-shot) move within about ±1% for larger models. Small models may dip. Zero-shot MMLU drops at most 1.7%.
  number: ±1%, 1.7%
  setup: 5-shot MMLU, 3-shot BBH, zero-shot MMLU
  quote: "For larger models, on the other hand, symbol tuning only results in performance changes within approximately ±1%"
  where: p.19. Zero-shot quote, p.20: "Symbol-tuned models saw a maximum decrease in performance of 1.7%"
- Benchmark noise: MMLU 5-shot for Flan-PaLM-8B moves with 1k-step increments of continued instruction tuning.
  number: 49.5 to 47.2 to 49.0
  quote: "continuing instruction-tuning on Flan-PaLM-8B for 1k steps reduces MMLU 5-shot performance from 49.5% to 47.2%, and continuing for another 1k steps improve performance back to 49.0%"
  where: p.20
- Symbol types: words-only symbols give the best flipped-label results at every size, and also beat integers on algorithmic tasks for 8B and 62B. Integers are not key for the algorithmic gains.
  number: flipped labels 54.8 (8B words), 54.2 (62B words), 59.8 (62B-c words), against 33.3, 30.7, 32.5 for integers
  setup: Table 3, no 540B
  quote: "using only words as labels results in the best performance on flipped labels"
  where: p.22
- Label space: ~30k labels is slightly better than 10-10k; larger label spaces help mostly 8B. Randomising the label mapping gives no gain (sanity check).
  number: none printed (read from Figures 15 and 16)
  quote: "models do not learn to better utilize in-context exemplars when symbol tuned using exemplars with randomized labels."
  where: pp.21-23

LIMITS
- Only Flan-PaLM models (8B to 540B) were tested, and the models are closed. It is not shown for GPT, Claude or open models.
- It is a finetuning method, not a prompting technique. The prompt-level takeaway is indirect. Evaluation prompts without instructions or labels are a stress test, not advice.
- Only classification-style, discrete-label tuning data. The authors say it is unclear how to include chain-of-thought data. CoT performance is "mostly consistent", but 8B drops significantly on BIG-Bench Hard with CoT after symbol tuning, unexplained (p.19).
- Gains shrink with scale (540B: +3.6 list functions, +4.7 Turing). Flipped-label accuracy is still not clearly better than chance on average. Small models overfit and lose accuracy when relevant labels exist.
- Evaluation is small: at most 100 examples per task, 11 tasks, 4-shot, single runs with no confidence intervals. The authors concede MMLU variance blurs the zero-shot conclusion.
- 540B declines after 1k steps, which the authors suggest means larger models need more or more diverse tuning data. The 540B model was excluded from the mixing, dataset-count, label-space, symbol-type and random-label ablations.
- Dated: Flan-PaLM-era (2022-23) models. Recent instruction-tuned models were not tested.

BUILDS ON
- Wei et al. 2023 (larger LMs do in-context learning differently): flipped-label finding that instruction tuning degrades flipped-label following.
- Min et al. 2022b: random labels in exemplars barely hurt performance, suggesting the label space drives performance.
- Chung et al. 2022 (Flan-PaLM) and Wei et al. 2022a (instruction tuning): base models and baseline.
- Brown et al. 2020 and Reynolds & McDonell 2021: prompt sensitivity.
- Madaan & Yazdanbakhsh 2022 and Wang et al. 2022: logically incorrect CoT prompts do not hurt.
- Garg et al. 2022, Akyürek et al. 2023, von Oswald et al. 2022 and Dai et al. 2023: in-context learning as learning algorithms.
- Webson & Pavlick 2022: models learn at the same rate with irrelevant or misleading prompts.
- Rajendran et al. 2020 and Yin et al. 2020: label augmentation, which the authors say symbol tuning resembles.
- Rule et al. 2020 and Telle et al. 2019 (task sources, via Srivastava et al. 2022, BIG-Bench).
- Raffel et al. 2020 (packing) and Shazeer & Stern 2018 (Adafactor).

CODE: none in the paper. The only code-like content is the prompt-format dumps in Appendix E (pp. 35-89), which I did not read. The Figure 1/4 prompt shapes are quoted below.
- Symbol-tuned prompt shape (p.3): "<sentence>. Answer: {Foo, Bar}"

FIGURES (captions from the text extraction; no images inspected)
- Fig 1 (p.1) and Fig 4 (p.5): side-by-side prompt layouts for instruction tuning (instruction plus "Positive/Negative") and symbol tuning (no instruction, "Foo/Bar"). Fig 4 shows all four instruction/relevant-label combinations. Best for explaining the idea quickly and for the "underspecified prompt" taxonomy, which also fits the target note on few-shot technique.
- Fig 3 (p.4): symbol categories (integers, characters, words). Fig 2 (p.3): the 22 tuning datasets by task type.
- Fig 5 (p.6): bars for list-function categories A-E and simple Turing concepts, base vs symbol-tuned, by model size.
- Fig 6 (p.7): flipped-label accuracy per dataset; instruction-tuned is far below chance and symbol-tuned recovers. This is the strongest picture of "prior vs in-context evidence".
- Fig 7-10 (pp.8-10): ablation curves (tuning steps, instruction-data mix, dataset count). Fig 14 (p.21): accuracy vs number of exemplars per class.
- Table 1 (p.5): the main results table; Table 2 (p.18): the continued-instruction-tuning control.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean text. Figures are charts, so their numbers exist only as plots and I quoted no figure-only numbers. Page markers are not in the extraction, so page numbers are from the printed page footers. No embedded instructions found in the PDF. I did not read the per-task tables in Appendix D or the prompt examples in Appendix E.
